title: The Seventh Bell
subtitle: The Legend of the Warden
teaser: Forty thousand men, the greatest siege-master who ever lived, and nine nights to move one stone giant out of a mountain pass. The Ash Khan tried everything, and the Warden kept all of it.

sections.heading: I. The Command
paragraphs: The mason-priests of Khal Dur spent forty years carving him out of the mountain. When they were finished, they climbed a ladder to his ear and gave him one command.
“Hold the pass.”
Then they climbed down, went home, and died one by one, the way priests do. Nobody ever came back to give him another.
For three hundred years, the most dangerous thing to come up the Pass of Seven Bells was a goat.

He stood in a niche in the cliff beside the gate, thirty feet of gray granite with a face like a shut door, so still that swallows nested in the crook of his arm. Snow sat on his shoulders all winter. The garrison hung their wet cloaks on his feet.

The pass took its name from its bells. Six hung in the watchtowers strung down the valley. The seventh, the great bell, hung in the arch of the gate itself, so big a man could stand up inside it. If anything ever came over the mountains, the bells would carry the warning down the valley faster than a horse.
Nobody living had heard them. The garrison oiled the ropes every spring and wondered why.
Then, in the three hundredth winter, the Ashen Host came over the snow.

They came at dusk, forty thousand strong, a black line across the white under the smoke of everything they had burned. The garrison rang all seven bells, and the warning rolled down the valley. Farms emptied. Carts filled. The whole valley ran south.
Captain Hesk looked at the forty thousand and did the sensible thing. His men did the sensible thing right behind him.
By full dark, the only thing left in the Pass of Seven Bells was the statue.

sections.heading: II. The Ash Khan
paragraphs: The man who led the Host had a name, but nobody in the valley ever learned it. They called him the Ash Khan, and he had never failed to take a wall.

He had taken the river city of Ossen by moving the river. He had taken the sea fort at Mur by waiting two years for a winter hard enough to freeze the sea, then walking across it. He had taken the Twin Gates of Calder by finding the one man inside who could be bought. Thirty-seven walls in all, and from each he had kept a single stone, in a cedar box that rode on a mule of its own.
He was a small man, neat and gray and quiet, and before every siege he set up a folding stool and drew the wall in charcoal, slowly, until he understood it. Then he took it.
He sat down in front of the Pass of Seven Bells and drew a gate, a cliff, and a statue in a niche. Then he sent the trebuchets.
The first stone brought the arch down. The great bell fell forty feet onto the rocks, split up one side, and rolled to a stop at the statue’s feet with one sour note.
Then the ram came up through the rubble, sixty men on the ropes.
The statue stepped out of the cliff.

It was the first step he had taken in three hundred years. Snow slid off him in sheets. The swallows burst from his arm. He walked into the broken gateway, set his feet where the gate had stood, and the ram took him square in the chest at a dead run.
The ram stopped. The sixty men did not, for a few more steps, and then they lay down in the snow and thought about it.
The Ash Khan rode up alone and looked at the giant with polite interest, the way he looked at every wall.
“Stand aside,” he said.
The giant’s voice was gravel poured down a well. It was the first thing he had said in three hundred years.
“Move me.”
The Khan considered this. Then he smiled, rode back to his stool, and turned to a fresh page.

sections.heading: III. Fire and Water
paragraphs: The Khan tried ropes first, cables as thick as a man’s waist looped around the Warden’s neck and arms, with two hundred oxen to pull them. The drovers whipped all night. Near dawn the Warden leaned forward, very slightly, and two hundred oxen went backward down the mountain.
“Everything moves,” the Khan told him the next evening. “Mountains move. Slowly, but they move.”
“Then be patient.”
“I am the most patient man alive.”
“I am three hundred years old,” said the Warden.

On the third night the Khan tried fire and water. He had every pine in the upper pass heaped around the Warden’s legs and burned it until the granite glowed. At dawn he would throw snowmelt over the hot stone and let the cold finish what the heat had started.

The Warden did not waste a good fire. He reached down, lifted the split bell out of the rubble, and laid it in the coals. All night, while the Host watched from the dark, he beat it on his own knee with his fist, and the pass rang like a smithy.
At dawn the water came down. The stone shrieked. Steam hid the gate, and when it cleared the Warden was still standing there, with a crack from his left shoulder to his hip and a hammer in his hands.
The head was the great bell, folded and beaten into a block the size of a hay cart. The haft was the iron bar of the fallen gate. When he set it down on the stones, it rang.
The Khan looked at the crack for a long time. He looked at the hammer longer.
“You’re welcome,” he said, and went back to his stool.

On the fourth night he sent three hundred sappers into the mountain to hollow out the ground beneath the giant’s feet. The Warden felt them all night, scratching in the dark like mice in a wall. Near midnight, as they fired the pit props to bring the tunnel down, he raised the hammer and brought it down once.

The mountain split. A crack opened at his feet and ran straight down the pass for a mile, and nobody has found the bottom. The tunnel went into it, and the trebuchets, and half the Khan’s baggage. The sappers came out of their holes a great deal faster than they had gone in.
Traders cross that crack today on a wooden bridge. They call it the Knock.

sections.heading: IV. The Thirty-Eighth Stone
paragraphs: On the fifth night the Khan sent his twelve best champions, one every hour. The Warden let each of them swing first, then swung once. He was careful with them. He had been told to hold the pass, not to empty it.
On the sixth night the Khan came up himself with forty mules behind him, and every mule was loaded with gold.
“Every wall I have ever taken,” he said, “had a man inside it who could be bought.”
“Then you’ve found one without.”
“So what are you, if you are not a man?”
The Warden thought about it. “In the way.”
The Khan left the gold in the snow anyway, in case it worked on the giant overnight, the way water works on stone.

On the seventh night the ash-priests of the Host sat down below the gate, gray with the ashes of their own dead, and sang to the stone of what it had been before it was a mountain: sand on the floor of a sea. The stone remembered. Cracks ran up the Warden’s legs like ice across a pond. Grit poured from his knees.
He lifted the hammer and struck the ground.

The mason-priests had cast that bell and blessed it, and it had hung three hundred years over the gate waiting for something worth ringing about. It rang now. The note went through the singers like a hand slapped flat on a table, and every one of them stopped at once.

On the eighth night the Khan stopped being clever and sent everything, and the Warden threw back his head and roared so loud that shepherds forty miles south thought the mountain was falling. He held the pass until dawn.
On the ninth night the Khan came alone, on foot, without his stool. He sat on the lip of the Knock with the cedar box in his lap.
“Thirty-seven,” he said, opening it. “A stone from every wall. I came here for the thirty-eighth.”
“I know.”
“Your soldiers ran. Your valley ran. The priests who gave you your orders are three hundred years dead. Why are you still here?”
The Warden was so cracked by then that pieces of him fell when he spoke.
“Three hundred years,” he said, “nothing came. Then you came.” There was a pause as long as weather. “Did you think I’d waste you?”
The Khan laughed until he had to wipe his eyes.

On the tenth morning the Host did not form up. The men stood at their fires looking up at the giant, and not one of them reached for a ladder. The Ash Khan knew armies the way he knew walls. He gave the only order to retreat of his life.
Before he rode north, he came up one last time and held out his hand.
“One chip,” he said. “Any piece. For the box.”
The Warden looked at the hand for a while.
“No,” he said.
The Ash Khan went home with thirty-seven stones and an empty place in the box, and they say he never filled it.

sections.heading: V. The Wall Walks Down
paragraphs: When the valley came home, it found the pass full of broken engines, a crack a mile long, forty mule-loads of gold lying in the snow, and the Warden standing in the gateway, cracked like a dropped plate, more or less where they had left him.

The smiths melted down the Khan’s gold and poured it into his cracks through a whole summer. So the bribe was spent on the Warden after all. The bands shine on him still, shoulder to hip, up both legs and across the brow, and you can read the whole war on him like a map.
The valley rang its six remaining bells every dawn for a hundred years, and every dawn, up in the pass, the seventh answered.

Then the ringers grew old, and the pass became a trade road. Traders hang their wet cloaks on his feet. Nothing has come over the snow since the Khan. The most dangerous thing in the Pass of Seven Bells is a goat again.
So one spring the Warden told the toll-keeper to ring if anything came, stepped out of the gateway, and walked down the mountain to find out whether anything could do what the Ash Khan couldn’t.

In the duelling rings he is the slowest thing anyone has ever fought, and it doesn’t matter. He doesn’t dodge. Blades skid off the stone and the gold. He walks through them the way he stood through nine nights, and when the hammer comes down it rings like a cracked bell, the ground jumps, and the floor of the ring tears open in a long fault line. Before a bout he roars, and the cheap seats feel it in their teeth.
The mason-priests of Khal Dur gave him one command, and he kept it. Now he has one of his own for anyone who steps into the ring with him. It is one word shorter than theirs.
